source.title: The p Factor: One General Psychopathology Factor in the Structure of Psychiatric Disorders?

confidence_rationale: The foundational, well-replicated empirical paper establishing the p factor (a single general-psychopathology dimension) in a 20-year longitudinal cohort. It grounds the EXISTENCE and transdiagnostic-loading premise of MECH-371's p-factor analogue -- a single broad vulnerability dimension that raises joint susceptibility across failure modes. Held at 0.72 because the paper validates the construct in humans but says nothing about MECH-371's specific MECHANISTIC interpretation (that the p-factor analogue IS control-plane / setpoint-regulation instability, ARC-005); that mapping is REE's own hypothesis and is not in the source.
failure_signatures: The p factor is a statistical/structural finding (a latent dimension that fits cross-disorder covariance better than separable factors); it does not identify a single causal mechanism, so MECH-371's claim that the analogue is specifically control-plane regulatory instability goes beyond what the source establishes and could be the wrong mechanistic identification.

p-factor structure can be partly an artefact of measurement and comorbidity-counting; a REE substrate that builds in a single global-instability scalar by construction risks manufacturing the dimension rather than discovering it -- the human evidence is for a latent factor, not for a designed-in scalar.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In the Dunedin longitudinal cohort followed from adolescence to midlife, the structure of psychopathology is captured better by a single general dimension (the p factor) than by separable Internalizing/Externalizing/Thought-Disorder factors. Higher p is associated with greater life impairment, greater familiality, worse developmental histories, and more compromised early-life brain function. The p factor explains why disorder-specific causes, biomarkers, and treatments are hard to find, and motivates transdiagnostic approaches.
mapping.ree_translation: Grounds MECH-371's central premise: that a single broad vulnerability dimension can load across ALL failure modes, raising joint susceptibility to many at once, orthogonal to any single-axis failure. The human p factor is the empirical referent for REE's 'global-instability / broad control-plane vulnerability axis' -- the one psychiatric-failure axis with no existing REE claim home -- and supports the prediction that a subset of agents carry elevated risk across the whole failure-mode space.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Caspi et al. establish that a general psychopathology dimension EXISTS and loads transdiagnostically; they do NOT identify its mechanism. MECH-371 additionally asserts the analogue is specifically instability in precision/gain/threshold setpoint regulation (ARC-005) -- a mechanistic identification the source neither makes nor tests. The source is human clinical-epidemiological data; REE's analogue is a control-plane-stability scalar in a synthetic agent. So the paper grounds the AXIS/transdiagnostic-loading claim, not the control-plane-mechanism claim.
mapping.source_context: Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study: ~1000-person birth cohort, psychiatric assessment across 20 years (adolescence to midlife); confirmatory factor analysis of disorder structure.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality high (landmark longitudinal cohort, definitive paper, heavily replicated since). Mapping fidelity moderate: grounds the existence + transdiagnostic-loading premise but not MECH-371's control-plane mechanistic identification. Transfer risk moderate: human clinical epidemiology to a synthetic global-stability scalar.
